sections.title: The three pillars & how to measure

items.q: How do metrics, logs, and traces differ, and when should each be used?
items.a:
The three pillars answer three different questions. Collapsing them into one answer usually signals a lack of production experience.
MetricsLogsTraces
Answersis something broken?what happened?where is it slow or failing?
Formnumbers aggregated over timediscrete, contextual eventsa tree of spans for one request
Costlow, roughly constant with traffichigh, grows linearlymoderate, thanks to sampling
Retentionyearsdays to weeksa few days
Best fordashboards, alerts, SLOsdetailed investigation and auditlocating bottlenecks across a service chain
The [[g:standard investigation flow]] is: a metric triggers an alert (p99 spikes) → a trace identifies the slow span → that span's logs explain why. :::deep - a [[r:common mistake]] is deriving metrics from logs, such as counting error lines to alert. It is expensive, slow, and breaks when logs are rate-limited. The code should emit counters and histograms directly. - a metric is a [[o:lossy aggregation]]: it cannot identify one specific request. That is the trace's job. - an [[g:exemplar]] in Prometheus and OTel attaches a trace ID to a histogram observation, allowing an operator to jump directly from a p99 spike on a dashboard to the trace that caused it. Mentioning this is a strong interview signal. - an emerging fourth pillar is [[o:continuous profiling]] with tools such as Pyroscope or Parca. It answers 'which line of code consumes CPU?', something a trace cannot reveal (21-linux-production-debug.jvm-network-deep-dive-on-prod.q3) - all three pillars should share the same labels (`service`, `env`, `version`) so operators can navigate between them In an OTA, flight-search p99 spikes → a trace shows that the GDS call consumes 90% of the request → the logs for that span reveal three retries after timeouts. Without a trace, the backend and integration teams can spend hours blaming each other. :::

items.q: How does OpenTelemetry propagate trace context across services and through message queues?
items.a:
**Concepts:** a [[b:trace]] represents the request's entire journey. Each leg is a [[b:span]] with the shared `trace_id`, its own `span_id`, and a `parent_span_id` pointing to its parent. **Over HTTP** — W3C Trace Context uses a single header: 
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             ^  ^                                ^                ^
             |  trace-id (16 byte)               span-id          flags (01 = sampled)
             version
A receiving service reads `traceparent`, creates a child span, and injects the header into every downstream call. OTel auto-instrumentation handles this for `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, and JDBC without application-code changes. **Through a message queue** — this is where traces [[r:most often break]]. There is no HTTP header, so the context must travel in the Kafka or RabbitMQ [[g:message headers]]: - producer: `inject()` the context into record headers before sending - consumer: `extract()` it from the headers and create a new span whose parent is the producer span 
propagator.inject(Context.current(), record.headers(),
    (headers, k, v) -> headers.add(k, v.getBytes(UTF_8)));
:::warn Parent–child relationship trap With a queue, the consumer usually [[r:should not]] be a `child` of the producer: the producer may have returned long ago, and one message can fan out to several consumers. Use a [[g:span link]] instead of a parent relationship; otherwise a trace can last for hours and produce a meaningless waterfall. ::: :::deep - [[o:sampling]] can be head-based (decided by the first service; cheap, but prone to missing rare failures) or [[g:tail-based]] (decided after the trace completes, retaining every failed or slow trace; more expensive and requires a collector to gather all spans) - retain 100% of [[g:failed]] and [[g:slow]] request traces, while sampling the rest at a low rate. This is almost always the right configuration. - in-process context propagates through `ThreadLocal`, so it [[r:breaks when work moves to a thread pool]] or `CompletableFuture`. OTel provides an `Executor` wrapper; virtual threads (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4) make this substantially easier. - OTel separates the [[o:API]] that application code depends on from the [[o:SDK]] that configures export, so changing the backend from Jaeger to Tempo or Datadog does not require code changes - `trace_id` must flow into logs (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q4); it is what joins the three pillars - baggage propagates business context such as `tenant_id` across the entire chain, but [[r:do not put PII]] in it because it reaches every service, including third parties :::

items.q: How do RED and USE guide metric selection for services and resources?
items.a:
The two formulas complement each other. Applying each in the right place prevents the anti-pattern of measuring everything without knowing what to inspect.

[[g:RED]] — for **services** that handle requests:
- [[b:R]]ate — requests per second
- [[b:E]]rrors — failed requests per second and error ratio
- [[b:D]]uration — the distribution of processing time, using a histogram rather than an average

[[g:USE]] — for **resources** such as CPU, disks, pools, and queues:
- [[b:U]]tilization — percentage of time busy
- [[b:S]]aturation — queued demand, such as run queue, pool wait, or lag
- [[b:E]]rrors — failures in the resource itself

A minimum service dashboard has RED for critical endpoints plus USE for the connection pool, thread pool, and consumer lag.

:::tip A useful closing line
*'High utilization is not necessarily painful; [[o:saturation]] is what the customer experiences.'* A CPU at 90% with an empty run queue is healthy—it is using the capacity you paid for.
:::

:::deep
- [[r:do not measure averages]]. An average of 200 ms may combine 95% of requests at 50 ms with 5% at 3 s. Use histograms and inspect p50/p95/p99.
- [[r:do not average percentiles]] across instances. Adding the p99 of ten pods and dividing by ten produces a meaningless number. Aggregate histogram buckets first, then calculate the percentile (`histogram_quantile` over `rate(..._bucket[5m])` performs that aggregation).
- measure latency [[o:separately for successes and errors]]: failed requests often fail fast and pull p99 down, hiding the real problem
- coordinated omission occurs when server-side measurement misses time spent waiting outside its queue; add client-side or load-balancer measurements
- useful Java-service saturation signals include `hikaricp.connections.pending`, thread-pool queue length, GC pause time, and Kafka consumer lag. These four catch most incidents.
- Google's [[g:four golden signals]] are RED plus saturation. Being able to connect both frameworks is sufficient.
:::

items.q: Why can one bad label cause a cardinality explosion that takes down the entire metrics system?
items.a:
[[b:Cardinality]] is the number of distinct time series. Prometheus stores **one series for every label combination** and keeps all active series in RAM. 
# 1 series — safe
http_requests_total{service="booking"}
#
# 5 endpoints x 4 statuses x 3 methods = 60 series — still safe
http_requests_total{service="booking", endpoint="/bookings", status="200", method="POST"}
#
# + user_id (1 million users) = 60,000,000 series — failure
http_requests_total{service="booking", ..., user_id="u_8412773"}
[[r:Labels with unbounded values]] are almost always the cause: `user_id`, `booking_id`, `email`, `trace_id`, full URLs containing path IDs, or exception messages. **Prevention:** - label values must come from a [[g:finite, known set]] - normalise paths to `/bookings/{id}`, not `/bookings/8H2K`; [[r:this is the most common mistake]] - high-dimensional analysis by user or booking belongs in [[g:logs or traces]], not metrics - configure `sample_limit` in the scrape configuration so one broken service cannot take down all of Prometheus :::deep - a quick estimate: a metric's cardinality is the [[o:product]] of the value counts for all labels. Adding a label with ten values multiplies cardinality by ten; it does not add ten. - symptoms include steadily growing Prometheus RAM until OOM, progressively slower queries, and increasing `scrape_duration`. Diagnose with `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` and the `/api/v1/status/tsdb` endpoint. - using an exception message as a label is a subtle trap: `error="connection timeout to 10.0.3.41:5432"` makes each IP and port combination a new series. Use a classified [[g:error type]] such as `error="timeout"`. - histogram `le` buckets also multiply cardinality: a 12-bucket histogram creates 12 series plus two. Do not add a histogram to an already highly labeled metric. - continuous deployments plus a `version` label create churn because old series consume RAM until retention expires. Consider removing version from high-frequency metrics. - in systems billed by custom metric, such as Datadog or CloudWatch, a cardinality explosion may not crash the platform; it [[r:explodes the bill]], sometimes discovered a month later :::

items.q: What decisions should SLI, SLO, SLA, and an error budget drive?
items.a:
- [[b:SLI]] (Indicator) — a measured value, such as the *percentage of successful requests completed within 300 ms*
- [[b:SLO]] (Objective) — an internal target, such as *99.9% over 30 days*
- [[b:SLA]] (Agreement) — a customer commitment with [[o:financial penalties]]. It is always looser than the SLO.
- [[b:Error budget]] = 100% − SLO. At 99.9% over 30 days, [[g:43 minutes and 12 seconds]] of failure are allowed.

The error budget is the actionable part: it turns the argument *"ship features or improve stability?"* into a [[g:data-driven decision]].

- budget remains → continue shipping and accept risk
- budget is exhausted → [[r:freeze feature work]] and focus the team on reliability

Choose SLOs around the [[o:user experience]], not resources. 'CPU below 80%' is not an SLO because customers do not care about CPU.

:::warn Do not set a 100% SLO
99.99% costs many times more than 99.9% and is rarely needed. An excessively high SLO keeps the error budget permanently exhausted, teaching the team to ignore it—which is worse than having no SLO.
:::

:::deep
- measure the SLO at the [[g:point closest to the user]], such as the load balancer or client side, not inside the service; internal measurement misses network and load-balancer failures
- distinguish [[o:request-based]] SLIs (ratio of good requests) from [[o:window-based]] SLIs (ratio of good minutes). Window-based measurement suits low-traffic services where a handful of failures makes the request ratio volatile.
- burn rate is the rate at which budget is consumed. A burn rate of 1 exhausts the budget exactly at the end of the period; 14.4 exhausts it in two days, making that an appropriate paging threshold (20-observability-sre.slos-alerting-incidents.q2).
- use different SLOs for different endpoints: booking a ticket (99.95%) deserves a tighter target than viewing history (99.5%). Combining them hides what matters.
- your SLO [[r:cannot exceed]] the product of the SLOs of its dependencies unless you provide graceful degradation
- in fintech, distinguish *failure* from *incorrect money*. A 0.1% error rate may be acceptable, but an incorrect balance has a zero budget; use invariants and reconciliation rather than the SLO framework for that case (topic 9).
:::

items.q: How should alerts be designed to avoid fatigue: should they fire on symptoms or causes?
items.a:
[[g:Alert on symptoms]] that hurt users, and [[r:do not page on causes]] such as high CPU or a restarted pod. There are hundreds of possible causes, most of which self-heal; there are few user-visible symptoms, and they are worth waking someone at 3 a.m. Paging on 'CPU at 90%' while customers can still buy tickets wastes attention. A few such pages teach the entire team to disable notifications. **Three levels, distinguished by urgency:**
LevelConditionDestination
Pagemoney or customers are being lost and someone must act nowphone call / wake-up
Ticketmust be handled during the day but is not yet affecting customerswork queue
Infouseful only during an investigationdashboard, no notification
**Burn-rate alerts** instead of static thresholds are the Google SRE standard: - burn rate ≥ [[o:14.4]] for 1 hour → **page** (the budget will be exhausted in two days) - burn rate ≥ [[o:6]] for 6 hours → **page** - burn rate ≥ [[o:1]] for 3 days → **ticket** A short window catches severe incidents; a long window catches slow leaks. Combining both gives fast detection with few false alarms. :::deep - every alert [[g:must]] link to a runbook containing the symptom, confirmation steps, the first three actions, and the escalation path. An alert without a runbook will be ignored. - if an alert [[r:requires no action twice in a row]], tune its threshold or delete it. Removing an alert is an improvement, not a failure. - configure `for: 5m` in Prometheus so the condition must persist, filtering transient noise - use [[o:inhibition]] and grouping: when an entire cluster fails, send one alert rather than 200. Alertmanager supports this, but it must be configured. - measure the alerting system itself: pages per week, out-of-hours ratio, and false-positive ratio. More than two pages per week for one on-call engineer is [[r:unsustainable]]. - also alert on [[o:'abnormal silence']]: throughput dropping to zero is often more serious than a high error ratio, yet an error threshold will not detect it :::

items.q: What is the incident-response process from the initial page through the postmortem?
items.a:
**During the incident — absolute priority order:**

1. [[g:Restore service first; investigate root cause later]]. Roll back immediately if a deployment just occurred. Do not debug in the middle of the fire.
2. **Assign explicit roles**: Incident Commander (coordinates and [[r:does not implement fixes]]), Ops (executes changes), and Comms (updates customers and internal stakeholders).
3. Use **one channel** and maintain a continuous timeline. The later postmortem then takes 20 minutes instead of half a day.
4. **Mitigate**: roll back · disable the feature with a flag · scale capacity · isolate the failing dependency with a circuit breaker · degrade deliberately.

**After the incident — a [[o:blameless]] postmortem:**

- timeline: when detection occurred, who did what, and when service was restored
- impact: number of users, money affected, and error budget consumed
- root causes explored with the [[g:five whys]]
- action items **with an owner and a deadline**; a postmortem without actions is merely an essay

:::warn Why it must be blameless
If people fear blame, they hide details and you lose precisely the information needed most. The right question is not *'who caused it?'* but *'why did the system allow an ordinary action to produce this outcome?'*
:::

:::deep
- track [[b:MTTD]] (detection), [[b:MTTA]] (acknowledgment), and [[b:MTTR]] (recovery). Improving MTTD is often the [[o:cheapest and most effective]] intervention because many long incidents simply went undetected for too long.
- there is rarely [[r:one root cause]]. Major incidents are almost always a chain in which several defensive layers fail together, the Swiss-cheese model.
- divide action items into [[g:reducing recurrence probability]] and [[g:reducing detection/recovery time]]. The second category is often more valuable because it also helps with incidents that have never occurred before.
- [[o:practice]] with game days, chaos engineering, and—most importantly—regular rollback tests. A rollback never tested will fail exactly when it is needed.
- fintech and OTA systems need [[o:post-incident reconciliation]]. Restored service does not imply correct data. Stuck bookings and debited payments without issued tickets must be scanned and resolved separately.
- describing a real incident with this structure—symptom → mitigation → cause → corrective action—is one of the strongest answers in a senior interview
:::

items.q: How should structured logging and correlation be designed so logs are actually searchable?
items.a:
A prose log line (`"user 42 failed to book seat 12A"`) is readable only by a person. [[g:Structured]] JSON logs are queryable: 
{"ts":"2026-07-31T10:04:12Z","level":"WARN","service":"booking",
 "trace_id":"4bf92f3577b34da6","span_id":"00f067aa0ba902b7",
 "event":"seat_hold_failed","seat":"12A","flight":"VN231",
 "reason":"already_held","duration_ms":42}
Every line has three [[o:mandatory]] elements: `trace_id` for linking to a trace, `service` plus `version`, and `level`. **Correlation** — place `trace_id` in MDC once at the inbound filter, and every subsequent log line carries it automatically: 
MDC.put("trace_id", Span.current().getSpanContext().getTraceId());
try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.clear(); }
`finally { MDC.clear(); }` is [[r:mandatory]] because pool threads are reused; without cleanup, the next request inherits the previous request's trace ID. :::deep - [[r:never log]] passwords, ID tokens (see the repository's Security section), card numbers, CVVs, or national identity numbers. Configure masking at the appender layer rather than relying on every developer's discipline. - log levels must retain their meaning: `ERROR` means [[o:a human needs to investigate]]. If an ERROR appears 10,000 times per day and no one reviews it, it is a `WARN`. Log-level inflation breaks every log-based alert. - use [[g:log sampling]] on high-frequency paths: retain 100% of failure logs and 1% of success logs. In large systems, logging often costs more than compute. - do not log and rethrow the same exception (`log.error(...); throw e;`) because one failure then produces five lines. Log in [[o:one place]], where it is actually handled. - write to `stdout` for the K8s or Docker runtime to collect; [[r:do not write and rotate files yourself]] inside a container - once `trace_id` exists, each line does not strictly need to repeat `user_id` and `booking_id`, but including them is still useful because logs commonly outlive traces - in Java, use `logstash-logback-encoder` for JSON or an OTel log appender to export directly over OTLP :::
